passage: You want to know why we borrowed? My name is Farida, and I'm Ishita's mother. When they asked for "a little gift" for her wedding, I said yes before my husband finished his tea. What if her in-laws were unkind to her? What if this proposal went and no one else came? So we borrowed from relatives and from the society, and paid for the hall, the furniture and the gold. My husband stopped sleeping. Two years on we are still paying, and a remark about "not enough" still comes now and then. I don't say it was foolish; it was love and fear. But I've thought: if five or six families in our lane had said no together, none of us would have borrowed. Now I tell my young neighbour Nazia: ask early, and ask together.

qa.q: What did Farida and her husband pay for?
qa.a: They paid for the hall, the furniture and the gold, using money borrowed from relatives and from the society.

qa.q: What was Farida afraid of when she said yes so quickly?
qa.a: Farida was afraid that her daughter's in-laws would be unkind to her and that no other proposal would come. Love and fear pushed her to agree.

qa.q: What turning point does Farida describe in her thinking, and what does she do about it?
qa.a: She realised that if several families in the lane had said no together, nobody would have borrowed. Now she tells her young neighbour Nazia to ask early and ask together.

qa.q: How was Farida's husband affected by the borrowing?
qa.a: He stopped sleeping, which shows the strain and worry it put on him.

grounding: A bride's mother agrees to demands and borrows heavily from fear for her daughter, and later sees that many families saying no together would change things.

passage: I live two doors from Uday, so I saw a lot last spring. First a list came from the groom's side. Then the tempo delivering the fridge and bed on it, then the bank man visiting twice about Uday's loan, then Uday selling the small plot behind the house. At the tea stall he kept telling everyone, "My Rani will be comfortable, that's all I want." He smiled every time, but he stopped ordering his usual second cup and left early. His wife Sushila carried boxes of sweets around the lane with her head high. On the wedding day Uday held his daughter for a long time. I can't say what was in his head. Maybe fear of a bad ending for Rani. Whatever it was, it cost him the plot. Four families in our lane did the same that year. Only Meher Aunty sent back her daughter's list and called the custom poison for daughters' families. Kunal

qa.q: What did Uday sell?
qa.a: Uday sold the small plot behind the house.

qa.q: What might Uday be feeling when he smiles but leaves the tea stall early, and how sure can Kunal be?
qa.a: Uday may be worried and strained under the smile, though Kunal cannot be sure. It is only a guess from the missing second cup and the early exits.

qa.q: Which choice did Uday make to secure Rani's comfort, and what did it cost him?
qa.a: He took a bank loan and sold the small plot behind the house to meet the list, hoping to make sure Rani would be comfortable.

qa.q: How does Sushila seem to carry herself, and what might that show?
qa.a: She carries sweets around the lane with her head high. It might be pride, or it might cover worry, and Kunal cannot tell which.

grounding: A bride's parents take on debt and sell property to meet expectations out of love and fear for their daughter, seen by a neighbour.

passage:
I didn't understand how much my parents had borrowed until after my wedding.
The groom's family never said a number. They said, "Your daughter should come with dignity." My mother, Ganga, heard that as a warning. She'd seen her own sister sent back home over a missing necklace. So Amma and Appa took a loan against our house and another from a moneylender in the market.
I was twenty-four. I saw the jewellery and the new furniture and I said nothing. I told myself it was their choice. The truth is I was afraid too, of being the daughter nobody would marry.
Now I watch Appa work extra shifts at sixty. Last month my younger cousin's family started getting the same hints. I went to my aunt's house and told her everything: the loans, the fear, the shifts. She listened. Then she said, "Vasudha, help me say no."

qa.q: Where did Amma and Appa take their second loan from?
qa.a: They took another loan from a moneylender in the market.

qa.q: Why did Vasudha say nothing when she saw the jewellery?
qa.a: Vasudha was afraid of being the daughter nobody would marry, so she stayed silent and told herself it was her parents' choice, though she now feels regret.

qa.q: What small step did Vasudha take that could help change the custom?
qa.a: Vasudha told her aunt the full truth about the loans and fear, so her cousin's family could refuse the hints; when more families say no, the pressure weakens.

qa.q: How might Ganga have felt when the groom's family talked about dignity?
qa.a: Ganga probably felt frightened and protective, remembering her sister being sent home over a missing necklace, and wanted to shield her daughter at any cost.

grounding: It shows a bride's family borrowing heavily out of fear that their daughter will be mistreated, and the bride helping another family say no.

passage:
Supervisor's note, accounts office, 12 November.
Uma, 26, one of our steadiest staff, asked me for a large salary advance today, the second this year. When I asked gently what it was for, she said it was for her younger sister's wedding. The groom's family had asked for a car "as a token of love," and her father, Bhupen, had already borrowed from two relatives.
Uma said, "If we don't give it, they'll treat my sister badly after the wedding. Papa is scared. I'm scared."
She looked exhausted. I did not lecture her. I told her that what she described sounded like dowry, and that her fear made sense. I gave her the number of the women's helpline and of the family counselling centre near the office. She said she would call the helpline with her father this evening. I have not approved the advance yet and will check in with her tomorrow.

qa.q: What did the groom's family ask for?
qa.a: The groom's family had asked for a car "as a token of love."

qa.q: What is Uma afraid of?
qa.a: Uma is afraid that if the family does not give the car, her sister will be treated badly after the wedding; she and her father are both scared.

qa.q: How did the supervisor support Uma well?
qa.a: The supervisor listened without lecturing, said her fear made sense, named what she described as dowry and gave her the helpline and counselling numbers, then planned to check in the next day.

qa.q: What would change if more families like Uma's refused such requests?
qa.a: If many families said no together, grooms' families could not count on fear, and daughters like Uma's sister would be less at risk.

grounding: It shows a family borrowing to meet a groom's demand out of fear for a daughter, and the need for families to seek help and say no.

passage:
Wednesday
Papa signed the loan papers today. I sat next to him at the bank and I signed too, as guarantor. Didi's wedding is in six weeks and the groom's side "hopes" for a proper reception, gold for the mother-in-law, and a bike. Papa kept saying, "What if they refuse her? What if they're cruel to her later?"
I didn't argue. I love Didi. I'm scared for her too.
But on the bus home I thought: if they're already asking this much, will a bike make them kind?
Called Eshaan tonight. His sister's in-laws never asked for anything and his family said no to one who did. He said, "Your Papa is being brave in the wrong direction."
Tomorrow I'm going to ask Didi what she wants. Not Papa. Not the aunties. Didi.
— Jagdish

qa.q: How long until Didi's wedding?
qa.a: Didi's wedding is in six weeks.

qa.q: What was Jagdish feeling while sitting next to Papa at the bank?
qa.a: Jagdish felt scared for Didi and loving toward her, but also doubtful, wondering on the bus whether a bike would ever make the in-laws kind.

qa.q: Why is asking Didi what she wants a wise next step?
qa.a: It puts the person whose life is at stake at the centre, instead of letting fear of the groom's side and the aunties decide for her.

qa.q: How does Eshaan see Papa's choice?
qa.a: Eshaan sees that Papa acts from love and courage, but that paying the demand strengthens a harmful custom, so he calls it being brave in the wrong direction.

grounding: It shows a bride's family borrowing to meet demands out of love and fear, and a family member beginning to question it.

passage:
Harsha: Arnab, you awake? can't sleep
Arnab: yes. what's up
Harsha: found out today Appa has pledged the farm land for Divya's wedding
Harsha: the groom's side keeps saying "no demands" but then "people will expect a good function, some gold, a bike for him"
Arnab: that's a demand
Harsha: I know. Appa says if we give less they'll treat her badly after. Amma is scared no one else will marry her. she's 24!
Arnab: they love her. that's why they're this scared
Harsha: I'm angry and I can't even be angry at them
Arnab: when my sister got married we said no to everything. my uncles fought us. but three families in our street did the same after that
Harsha: really?
Arnab: really. someone has to go first
Harsha: I'll talk to Divya tomorrow. if she's ready, we both talk to Appa. and to the groom directly
Arnab: I'll come if you want
Harsha: thanks da

qa.q: What has Appa pledged for Divya's wedding?
qa.a: The farm land.

qa.q: Why are Harsha's parents willing to take such a risk?
qa.a: They are frightened and loving, fearing Divya will be treated badly or remain unmarried if they give less.

qa.q: What step is Harsha planning, and why is it wise?
qa.a: Talking to Divya first and then, together, to Appa and the groom directly; it respects Divya's wishes and challenges the demand openly.

qa.q: What does Arnab's family story suggest about change?
qa.a: It suggests that when one family refuses, others find courage, since three families on his street did the same afterwards.

grounding: It illustrates a bride's parents borrowing heavily out of fear and love, and how social change needs families to say no.
